item.title: Public told not to be alarmed by military activity in West
item.description: People living in or travelling through parts of the Western Division have been advised not to be alarmed by military movements, blank ammunition and simulated battle sounds as the Republic of Fiji Military Forces begins a three-week training exercise today. The RFMF said Bougainville Exercise 2026 will be conducted in the vicinity of Nadi and Lautoka, including surrounding interior areas, from Mon
item.content:encoded:
People living in or travelling through parts of the Western Division have been advised not to be alarmed by military movements, blank ammunition and simulated battle sounds as the Republic of Fiji Military Forces begins a three-week training exercise today.

The RFMF said Bougainville Exercise 2026 will be conducted in the vicinity of Nadi and Lautoka, including surrounding interior areas, from Monday, August 10 to Friday, August 28.

The exercise will involve the movement of military personnel and vehicles through the affected areas.

The RFMF said blank ammunition and pyrotechnics will also be used to simulate battle noise as part of the training.

Members of the public residing in or travelling through the areas have been advised that the increased military presence and sounds associated with the exercise are part of planned training activities.

“The Republic of Fiji Military Forces (RFMF) wishes to inform members of the public that a training exercise will be conducted in the Western Division, in the vicinity of Nadi and Lautoka, including surrounding interior areas, from Monday, 10 August to Friday, 28 August 2026,” the RFMF said in its public notice.

It said people should not be alarmed if they encounter military personnel and vehicles or hear simulated battle sounds during the exercise.

“The exercise will involve the movement of military personnel and vehicles, as well as the use of blank ammunition and pyrotechnics for battle noise simulation,” the RFMF said.

“Members of the public residing in or travelling through these areas are kindly advised not to be alarmed by military movements or simulated sounds associated with the exercise.”

However, people have been asked to exercise caution while travelling through areas where the training is taking place.

The RFMF said preparations had been undertaken to reduce any potential risks associated with the exercise.

“The RFMF has undertaken the necessary planning and safety measures to minimise risks to the public and ensure that the exercise is conducted safely and professionally,” it said.

The military has not detailed the specific locations within the Nadi and Lautoka areas where individual training activities will take place.

The RFMF thanked members of the public for their understanding and cooperation during the three-week exercise.

It also acknowledged the public’s continued support throughout the duration of Bougainville Exercise 2026.

item.title: Kumar calls for review of taxi fares, EFL fuel surcharge
item.description: Opposition Member of Parliament Premila Kumar has called on the Fijian Competition and Consumer Commission to immediately review temporary taxi fare increases and the electricity fuel surcharge following a fall in fuel prices. Kumar said consumers were required to absorb higher costs when fuel prices increased and should now receive relief when those costs fall.
item.content:encoded:
Opposition Member of Parliament Premila Kumar has called on the Fijian Competition and Consumer Commission to immediately review temporary taxi fare increases and the electricity fuel surcharge following a fall in fuel prices.

Kumar said consumers were required to absorb higher costs when fuel prices increased and should now receive relief when those costs fall.

“When fuel prices went up, consumers were told that higher prices were unavoidable because of international fuel costs,” Kumar said.

“Now that fuel prices have fallen, consumers should not be told that the increases must remain because international prices are ‘volatile’.”

She said the FCCC had approved a temporary taxi fare increase from July 1, 2026, which increased the distance charge for general taxis from 10 cents to 14 cents per 100 metres.

For Nadi Airport taxis, the distance charge increased from 15 cents to 21 cents per 100 metres.

“Consumers immediately felt the impact. But if the fuel cost pressures that justified the increase have eased, why should passengers continue paying the higher fare?” Kumar questioned.

“A temporary increase cannot become a permanent increase simply because consumers have already been made to pay it.”

Kumar said the same principle should apply to the electricity fuel surcharge.

She said the FCCC had allowed Energy Fiji Limited to impose a 5.91 cents per kilowatt-hour fuel surcharge on households earning $30,000 or less.

At the same time, she said Government provided EFL with a four-month fuel rebate of 20 cents per litre for diesel and 12 cents per litre for heavy fuel oil.

“Now that the fuel prices have fallen, when will consumers see the benefit?” she asked.

Kumar said electricity and transport were essential expenses that families could not easily avoid.

“Families cannot switch off their electricity because the bill is too high. They cannot simply choose not to travel to work or hospital because taxi fares have increased. These are essential costs.”

She said households were already under pressure from the cost of food, transport, electricity and other necessities, and additional charges placed further strain on family budgets.

Kumar said regulation needed to work in both directions when underlying costs changed.

“You cannot use volatility to justify increases when prices rise and then ignore falling prices when prices come down,” she said.

“If fuel prices rise again, the FCCC can review the situation again. That is precisely why these measures were described as temporary.”

Kumar said the principle should be straightforward.

“When costs rise, consumers may have to bear some of the increase. When those costs fall, consumers must also receive the benefit.”

“Otherwise, ‘temporary’ becomes another word for permanent.”

She called on the FCCC to immediately reassess both measures in light of lower fuel prices.

“Consumers should not be expected to carry the burden when prices go up while service providers retain the benefit when prices come down,” Kumar said.

item.title: Cash remains king for majority of Fijians
item.description: Cash remains the preferred method of payment for most Fijians despite the growing availability of mobile money, internet banking and other digital financial services, according to the Fiji Financial Services Demand Side Survey 2025. The survey found that 60 per cent of Fijians prefer using cash, while 36 per cent prefer digital payments but do not know how to use them.
item.content:encoded:
Cash remains the preferred method of payment for most Fijians despite the growing availability of mobile money, internet banking and other digital financial services, according to the Fiji Financial Services Demand Side Survey 2025.

The survey found that 60 per cent of Fijians prefer using cash, while 36 per cent prefer digital payments but do not know how to use them.

Only a small proportion indicated a clear preference for digital payments.

The preference for cash was relatively consistent between men and women, with 59 per cent of males and 61 per cent of females preferring cash.

However, significant differences emerge when the figures are broken down by age.

Younger Fijians were more open to digital payments, with only 55 per cent of those aged 15 to 35 preferring cash.

Cash preference increased to 56 per cent among those aged 36 to 55 before climbing sharply among older Fijians.

About 78 per cent of people aged 56 to 65 preferred cash, rising further to 82 per cent among those aged 66 and above.

There were also considerable geographical differences.

The Northern Division recorded the strongest preference for cash at 70 per cent, followed by the Western Division at 65 per cent and Eastern Division at 63 per cent.

In the Central Division, only 52 per cent preferred cash, while 43 per cent said they preferred digital payments but did not know how to use them.

Rural residents were also considerably more likely to favour cash, with 68 per cent preferring cash compared with 54 per cent of urban residents.

The survey found convenience was the biggest reason people continued using cash.

Among those who preferred cash, 42 per cent said it was because cash was easy to use, while 25 per cent said merchants and stores mainly used cash.

Another 16 per cent used cash to avoid bank charges or fees, while 13 per cent preferred it for emergencies.

Despite the strong preference for cash, the survey indicates there is potential for greater digital payment adoption if barriers to usage are addressed.

People with disabilities were significantly more likely to report preferring cash because they did not know how to use digital banking services or experienced difficulty using them.

Among Fijians aged over 66, 67 per cent reported lower education levels and 60 per cent experienced significant difficulty using digital services, making electronic payments particularly challenging for this group.

The survey also found that while 39 per cent of people over 66 preferred cash for all payments, 59 per cent would consider not using cash in certain situations.

Overall, just 40 per cent of Fijians using formal financial services preferred digital payments over cash, highlighting the continued dominance of physical currency despite Fiji’s expanding digital financial landscape.

item.title: Court reveals details of local boat operator’s role in Vatia drug bust
item.description: A boat operated by Nadi businessman Anand Kumar was allegedly used to transport 2.6 tonnes of cocaine from a narco-submarine originating from Ecuador to Fiji, according to a High Court ruling. The allegation was detailed by Justice Samuela Qica in his July 31 ruling refusing Kumar’s application for bail pending trial.
item.content:encoded:
A boat operated by Nadi businessman Anand Kumar was allegedly used to transport 2.6 tonnes of cocaine from a narco-submarine originating from Ecuador to Fiji, according to a High Court ruling.

The allegation was detailed by Justice Samuela Qica in his July 31 ruling refusing Kumar’s application for bail pending trial.

According to the court, Kumar operates boat hire and game fishing charter services from Nadi under the business name Giant Trevally Fishing.

It is alleged that a boat used in his business was used to load cocaine from a narco-submarine originating from Ecuador before transporting the drugs to Vatia Wharf in Tavua.

The alleged operation took place in January this year, while Kumar was formally charged on June 4.

Kumar faces one count of unlawful importation of illicit drugs, one count of unlawful possession of illicit drugs and one count of possession of property suspected of being proceeds of crime.

The court was told the illicit drug was allegedly cocaine weighing 2.6 tonnes.

In considering Kumar’s bail application, Justice Qica described the quantity involved as “enormous”.

He said the allegation was that Kumar’s business vessel had been used as the means of bringing drugs from a foreign narco-submarine onto Fijian soil.

The judge noted the case formed part of a wider investigation involving other accused persons, some of whom had already been refused bail.

The State told the court investigations were continuing and there was a risk of interference with witnesses if Kumar was released.

Kumar, however, claimed during his caution interview that he had acted as an informant for foreign agents and local police and had been working undercover.

The State maintained there was no written authority permitting the transfer of illicit drugs using Kumar’s vessel.

Justice Qica said the case allegedly involved a sophisticated transnational operation and found that the risk of interference with evidence or witnesses could not be dismissed.

“The public interest in the proper investigation and prosecution of large-scale drug importation and possession offences is of the highest order,” Justice Qica said.

He also highlighted Fiji’s geographical position and the documented use of its maritime approaches by international trafficking networks as factors weighing heavily in favour of protecting the community.

Justice Qica ultimately found there remained a material risk Kumar would not surrender to custody given the gravity of the charges and potential sentence.

The court refused bail, although Kumar remains entitled to file a fresh or review application or appeal the decision.

item.title: Justice Tuiqereqere to deliver landmark COI ruling today
item.description: High Court judge Justice Dane Tuiqereqere is expected to deliver a landmark judgment today in separate judicial review proceedings challenging findings made in the Commission of Inquiry report into the appointment of former FICAC Commissioner Barbara Malimali. The matters are listed for judgment before Justice Tuiqereqere in High Court Room 13 at 9am today, Monday, August 10.
item.content:encoded:
High Court judge Justice Dane Tuiqereqere is expected to deliver a landmark judgment today in separate judicial review proceedings challenging findings made in the Commission of Inquiry report into the appointment of former FICAC Commissioner Barbara Malimali.

The matters are listed for judgment before Justice Tuiqereqere in High Court Room 13 at 9am today, Monday, August 10.

The judicial review proceedings involve former FICAC Commissioner Barbara Malimali, former Attorney-General Graham Leung, Fiji Law Society president Wylie Clarke and lawyer Laurel Vaurasi.

The applicants have separately challenged findings made against them arising from the Commission of Inquiry into Malimali’s appointment as Commissioner of the Fiji Independent Commission Against Corruption.

Malimali’s proceeding, HBJ 09/2025, names the Commission of Inquiry into her appointment, the President of Fiji, the Prime Minister and the Attorney-General as respondents.

A separate proceeding, HBJ 10/2025, has been brought by Wylie Clarke and Laural Vaurasi.

They have also named the Commission of Inquiry, the President, the Prime Minister and the Attorney-General as respondents and are represented by Howards Lawyers.

Graham Leung’s proceeding, HBJ 11/2025, names the Commission of Inquiry and the Attorney-General as respondents.

The judgment is significant because it will determine the legal challenges brought by the four applicants over findings concerning them in the Commission of Inquiry report.

The Commission of Inquiry was established to investigate circumstances surrounding Malimali’s appointment as FICAC Commissioner.

Today’s judgment is expected to provide clarity on the applicants’ challenges to the Commission’s findings and the legal standing of those findings.

The three matters are listed consecutively before Justice Tuiqereqere for judgment.

item.title: LTA introduces mandatory learner course
item.description: THE Land Transport Authority (LTA) is introducing a mandatory Learner Driver Course (LDC) for all Class 2 Learner Permit applicants from tomorrow (Monday). The new requirement is aimed at strengthening driver education and improving road safety outcomes in Fiji.
item.content:encoded:
THE Land Transport Authority (LTA) is introducing a mandatory Learner Driver Course (LDC) for all Class 2 Learner Permit applicants from tomorrow (Monday).

The new requirement is aimed at strengthening driver education and improving road safety outcomes in Fiji.

LTA chief executive officer Irimaia Rokosawa said applicants must successfully complete the free course before they can sit the Driver Knowledge Test (DKT).

The course will be available at all LTA branches nationwide.

Applicants who successfully complete the course will receive an LDC Advice Slip, which must be presented before they are allowed to undertake the DKT.

Mr Rokosawa said the initiative was designed to give new drivers a stronger foundation in road safety, traffic laws, and responsible driving.

“The introduction of the mandatory Learner Driver Course reflects the authority’s commitment to ensuring new drivers begin their licensing journey,” he said.

He said the course would provide new drivers with a strong understanding of road safety principles, the P1 and P2 licensing system, show-cause proceedings, digital logbooks, responses to accidents and emergencies, traffic laws and the responsibilities that come with operating a motor vehicle.

Mr Rokosawa said driving was a privilege that carried significant responsibility.

“Before an individual gets behind the wheel, they must understand not only the road rules, but also the consequences of unsafe decisions and behaviours on the road.”

The course will cover road rules, traffic signs and signals, driver responsibilities, hazard awareness, defensive driving, and safe road-user behaviour.

Learner drivers will also be taught about the importance of sharing the road safely with pedestrians, cyclists, motorcyclists, and other motorists.

Mr Rokosawa said many road crashes were preventable and were often linked to poor decision-making, inadequate knowledge of road rules and unsafe driving behaviour.

item.title: Pacific looks to renewable energy
item.description: THE ongoing fuel crisis has prompted Pacific leaders to look more closely at strengthening renewable energy solutions across the region. Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) Secretary General Baron Waqa said the issue was discussed by Pacific Foreign Ministers as leaders considered ways to strengthen the region’s response to the ongoing repercussions of the conflict in the Middle East.
item.content:encoded:
THE ongoing fuel crisis has prompted Pacific leaders to look more closely at strengthening renewable energy solutions across the region.

Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) Secretary General Baron Waqa said the issue was discussed by Pacific Foreign Ministers as leaders considered ways to strengthen the region’s response to the ongoing repercussions of the conflict in the Middle East.

Mr Waqa said the fuel crisis was one of the priority areas being addressed through the regional response mechanism established by Pacific leaders through the Troika (a pacific leadership group that provides strategic guidance and maintains regional continuity between annual summits).

“I think what is important to understand is that this crisis, we have no control over, all right, the effects of it,” he said.

“So, what we can only do for ourselves is making sure that we help each other and arrive at a way of addressing.”

Mr Waqa said the effects of the crisis extended beyond fuel prices, affecting transportation costs, inflation, the cost of goods and the ability of people to afford their livelihoods.

Mr Waqa said Pacific leaders were also considering renewable energy as part of the region’s response.

“Also, as the Pacific is a leader in climate change and addressing issues regarding climate change, and one of them is renewable energy.”

item.title: Fiji’s $100m oil hit
item.description: RISING oil prices have already cost people and businesses in Fiji an estimated $F100million ($US45million) since the start of the Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz crisis, according to a new analysis by global grassroots environmental organisation, 350.org. The analysis estimates that the cost could exceed $F220million ($US100million) by the end of the year should the crisis continue to escalate.
item.content:encoded:
RISING oil prices have already cost people and businesses in Fiji an estimated $F100million ($US45million) since the start of the Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz crisis, according to a new analysis by global grassroots environmental organisation, 350.org.

The analysis estimates that the cost could exceed $F220million ($US100million) by the end of the year should the crisis continue to escalate.

Even if the Strait of Hormuz and the wider region return quickly to normal, higher oil prices would still cost people and businesses in Fiji more than $F144million ($US65million) by the end of the year, 350.org says.

The analysis is based on oil and gas pricing scenarios in the International Monetary Fund’s April 2026 World Economic Outlook, Fiji’s fuel consumption data and observed average prices since the start of the Iran war and Hormuz crisis.

Fenton Lutunatabua, 350.org Pacific and Caribbean program lead said the figures highlighted the uneven impact of rising fossil-fuel prices.

“It is shocking to see these obscene profit margins in global oil and gas companies, while people in Fiji are having to dig deeper into their pockets to pay for a crisis not of their making,” Mr Lutunatabua said.

“It has never been clearer that we need to break free of our reliance on imported fuel and invest in our own renewable energy independence.

“Across the Pacific, our people are being choked by climate disasters and rising costs of living. The just transition to renewable energy needs to happen swiftly, and I think the people who are profiting from our struggle, the world’s highest earners, and highest polluters, should be required to pay their fair share of it.”

The estimates do not account for wider economic effects, including higher fertiliser and food costs, lower economic output and employment, or increased inflation driven by fossil-fuel price volatility. The true economic impact could therefore be significantly greater than the direct cost of higher oil and gas prices.

The analysis comes as five of the world’s largest oil and gas companies reported a combined $US48billion in profits in their latest quarterly results: TotalEnergies, $US6billion; Shell, $US9.8billion; Chevron, $US12.1billion; ExxonMobil, $US14.5billion; and BP, $US5.7billion.

Most of the companies reported some of their highest profits since 2022.

Questions sent to Minister for Finance Esrom Immanuel remain unanswered when this edition went to press.
